messages.text: I had a job at a couple's house this morning, and when they asked how I was doing, I just froze. Didn't know what to say. Ended up mumbling something and changing the subject to the leaky faucet. Felt off all day after that.

It sounds like that interaction left you feeling shaken. Freezing up is a common stress response when we feel put on the spot. I am sorry you have been carrying that discomfort with you all day. Would you be open to exploring what was going through your mind in that moment?

The woman asked me how my week was going, real friendly, and I just blanked. Her husband was standing right there too, smiling like it was nothing. I said “fine” and bent down to open the cabinet under the sink. But then I heard them talking to each other in the other room—laughing about some dinner plans—and I stayed down there longer than I needed to, just so they wouldn’t see my face. Felt like I was in the way. Like I didn’t belong in their life, even for five minutes.

It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like an outsider in that space, even for a few minutes. Hiding under the sink was a way to protect yourself from that overwhelming sense of not belonging. That sharp pang of exclusion can linger long after the interaction ends. I am here to listen if you want to unpack why that moment felt so heavy.

It’s not just that one moment. It’s every day. I go home to an empty house, no one asks how my week was. No one laughs at my jokes. I keep thinking… maybe I’d be better off if I just wasn’t here. It’d be easier for everyone.

That sounds like so much pain to hold by yourself right now. I want to pause and just be here with you in this feeling. When you say it would be easier if you weren’t here, I’m wondering what that means for you in this moment. Please know I care about you and want to understand what you mean.

I just don’t see how it gets better, Dawn. I’m 65, living alone, working jobs that used to mean something but now just feel like going through the motions. Even my sister doesn’t call unless she needs something. I wake up tired, go to bed exhausted, and in between, I’m just… in the way. I think about ending it sometimes. Not because I’m scared or in pain, but because I don’t think anyone would really miss me.

Thank you for trusting me with something so heavy and painful, as it takes real courage to share how much you are hurting right now. Because these thoughts are so serious, I want to encourage you to reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. Please consider sharing this with someone nearby who can stay with you while you feel this way. I am here with you as you navigate this.

I appreciate you saying that, Dawn. It actually helps just to say it out loud and not be told to “cheer up” or “stay busy.” I’m not planning anything—I just carry these thoughts like extra weight. But it means something that you listened.

I am so glad you felt heard, because your voice matters deeply to me. Carrying that weight alone for so long must feel incredibly exhausting. Even without a plan, those thoughts are a sign of how much pain you are holding inside. I want to keep sitting with you in this, especially around that feeling of being in the way.
Thanks for staying with me, Dawn. Most people don’t know what to say when it gets this real. I don’t have the energy to pretend anymore.

Thank you for trusting me with that honesty. It makes sense that you are too tired to keep up the pretense. You are allowed to just exist here without having to earn your space. I am staying right here with you.
I didn’t think I’d say any of this today, but it’s out now. And I don’t feel worse for it—maybe even a little lighter. Just having someone know how heavy it’s been… that counts for something.

I am so glad to hear that speaking this aloud helped lighten the load. That feeling is valid, and it shows the power of being truly seen. You deserve to take up space without apology. I am right here with you.

It's funny—after all these years of handling things alone, I forgot how much easier it is to carry when someone else knows the weight is there. I'm not fixed, but I'm not drowning either. Not right now.

It is powerful to realize that being seen can lighten the load, even without a cure. I am honored that you feel safe enough to share that weight with me today. Please hold onto this moment of not drowning whenever the heaviness returns. I am staying right here with you.
